## Introduction

\[No abstract is needed.\] Each reproducibility project will have a straightforward, no frills report of the study and reproducibility results. These reports will be publicly available as supplementary material for the aggregate report(s) of the project as a whole. Also, to maximize project integrity, the intro and methods will be written and critiqued in advance of your attempt to reproduce the results. Introductions can be just 1-2 paragraphs clarifying the main idea of the original study, the target finding for your reproducibility attempt, and any other essential information. It will NOT have a literature review -- that is in the original publication. You can write both the introduction and the methods in past tense.

### Justification for choice of study

The paper by Salomons et al. explains the cognitive development of assistance puppies (aged 8 to 20 weeks) as measured through performance on a biweekly battery of 9 tasks: marker gesture, working memory, working memory with distraction, auditory discrimination, odor discrimination, cylinder (inhibitory control and reversal learning), unsolvable, causal reasoning, and momentary pointing. The results support the multiple intelligences hypothesis and suggest the emergence of distinct cognitive abilities, with clear developmental breakpoints in marker gesture comprehension, inhibitory control, reversal learning, and eye contact occurring before 16 weeks, coinciding with the period of rapid brain development. The goal of this project is to answer if different cognitive skills develop at different rates in assistance puppies. The authors, however, chose to model each task separately and compare developmental rate visually rather than test comparisons directly. Using data exclusively from the 91 longitudinal subjects, I will reproduce Figure 2 and directly test whether age-related improvement differs across tasks using an age × task interaction. Next, I will simulate additional data from the fitted model to test whether a study of this size (N=91) can reliably detect these differences or is a larger sample (N=1000) is needed for sufficient power.

I am currently working to develop a battery of tests that can be administered to large numbers of dogs, in the hopes of identifying exceptional performers and determining whether strong performance on one task may generalize across different measures of the same ability and/or across cognitive domains. Knowing when different skills emerge will inform when puppies should be tested, and between-task correlations will suggest whether performance may generalize across domains. With the help of citizen science, this method may ultimately identify exceptional dogs.

### Anticipated challenges

As explained above, my plan for this project includes (1) reanalyzing existing data from the 91 longitudinal puppies and (2) simulating additional subjects. My plan for this project will include 6 steps:

1.  Reproduce Figure 2 with LOESS curve
2.  Reproduce per-task models correct \~ age + (1 \| puppy_ID) and correct \~ age + experience + (1 \| puppy_ID)
3.  Confirmatory mixed-effects logistic model, correct \~ age \* task + (1 \| puppy_ID) + (1 \| puppy_ID:task)
    - Key result is age × task interaction (only including data from the 91 longitudinal subjects, so age and experience will confound)
    - Significant interaction supports multiple intelligences hypothesis
4.  Calculate (for how much faster one skill develops relative to another)
5.  Data simulation using fitted model (step 3) for N=91 vs N=1000
6.  Plot simulated data with LOESS curves like Figure 2

My reproduction will be successful if curves match Figure 2, betas are within +/- 0.01 of the reported, and a find the same best-AIC model per task. My simulation will be successful if slopes show little bias, I can get \~95% CI coverage, and \~80% power for interaction, ideally at N=91.

I anticipate running into a few challenges when attempting to reproduce these results. First, age and experience are highly intertwined since they increase together for all longitudinal subjects. In addition, many of the dogs are siblings, half-siblings, cousins, etc. and this relatedness is not included in the dataset and may be a confound. Finally, of the 11 measures, 10 are binary responses (score out of 4 trials) and one is average looking time, thus I am considering removing the last measure from my simulation for ease. The biggest challenge, however, will be actually completing this project given my minimal programming knowledge and experience.

### Learning Goals

- learn to fit and interpret mixed-effects models for the data
- learn how to write a simulation function that generates correlated data across all 11 measures for the same subject
- learn how to use simulation to test how sample size and testing schedule affect power (directly applies to planning my future project)

## Methods

### Description of the steps required to reproduce the results

1.  **Data Preparation.** Before I could begin my reproduction, I first had to prepare the data. The dataset included in the supplements of Salomons et al. does not include subject ID and thus, you cannot see how an individual dog performs across tests. To fix this error, I used an additional spreadsheet (from a Shared Drive I can still access from my undergrad) to map subject names to each row and assign arbitrary subject ID numbers. After cleaning the xlxs file, each task was exported as a separate CSV file.
2.  **Reproduce Figure 2.** Using the cleaned data, I filtered the each CSV to include only longitudinal subjects so I could reproduce Figure 2. For each of the 11 measures, I plotted proportion correct (or mean look time and proportion of trials looked for the unsolvable task) against age in weeks. Points were jittered for individual sessions, a LOESS smoothing curve was applied, and the 11 panels were combined into a single figure using the "patchwork" library.
3.  **Reproduce Per-Task Models.** For each binary-outcome task, I fit two mixed-effects logistic regression models, with a random intercept for subject: correct \~ age + (1 \| puppy ID) and correct \~ age + experience + (1 \| puppy ID), where experience is the number of prior test sessions. The unsolvable task was modeled as proportion of trials looked (logistic) and mean look time (linear). Outcomes were modelled as the number of correct trials out of the total trials in each session. Models were run, and compared, on the longitudinal subjects alone and on entire 113-dog sample. For each sample, the two models were compared using AIC, and the age and experience coefficients of the longitudinal+control models were compared with those reported in the original paper.
4.  **Confirmatory Age × Task Models.** The remainder of the analyses were completed using only binary-outcome tasks (i.e., excluding unsolvable task measures) and include only the longitudinal subjects (n=91). To test directly whether cognitive skills develop at different rates, I combined the nine binary-outcome tasks and fitted correct \~ age x task + (1 \| puppy ID) + (1 \| puppy ID:task) to the 91 longitudinal puppies, with age centred at 8 weeks. The key result is the age × task interaction, wherein a significant interaction indicates that tasks develop at different rates and supports the multiple intelligences hypothesis. Because age and experience are highly correlated in the longitudinal sample, this model cannot disentangle the effects of maturation and testing experience. I also examined the effects of adding a random puppy slope for age, refitting the model with all 113 puppies and task-specific experience effects to see if age can be separated from experience.
5.  **Calculate Effect Sizes.** Using the confirmatory model, I extracted per-task effect size (age slope as an odds ratio) and compared each task. Comparing effect sizes serves as a measure of how much faster one skill develops relative to another. Slopes were also expressed as the change in proportion correct per week.
6.  **Data Simulation.** Using both the fixed and random-effects confirmatory model, I will simulate trial-level data for each task. Simulations will be run for two different samples: a replication of original sample size (n=91) and a larger sample (n=1000), whose testing schedules will be resampled from the original puppies.
7.  **Plot Simulated Data.** Data from both the small and large simulations will be plotted in the same format as Figure 2 using jittered points and LOESS curves for each task. The simulated developmental trajectories can therefore be compared to the actual data and we can also observe the effects of increased sample size on the curves.

### Differences from original study

To complete my analyses, participant ID had to be reconstructed by matching the provided summary data to raw and cleaned DCLB datasets, and a few sessions differed slightly between the three sources. Given the large scope of the original study, I needed to greatly limit the breatdth of my analysis for this project. Unlike the original study, my models only include age and experience, ignoring the potential effects of age and rearing strategy. With this narrowing, I will focus primairly on the longitudnial subjects and will thus not reproduce the longitudinal vs control comparisons of Table 3 or the segmented regression of Table 4. Additionally, the majority of my analyses were not included in the original paper, namely the combined age x task model, random slopes, the model including control puppies, and between-task effect sizes. Finally, Salomons et al. used RStudio 2023.06.1 while my project will use 2026.10.0.

### Reproducibility

#### Individual Plots

```{r auditory_plot}
auditory_long <- auditory |>
  filter(Status=="Longitudinal") |>
   mutate(
    `Age (wks)` = as.numeric(`Age (wks)`),
    `Proportion Correct` = as.numeric(`Proportion Correct`),
     `experience` = as.numeric(`# Prior Test Sessions`)
  )

auditory_plot <- auditory_long|>
  ggplot(aes(x=`Age (wks)`, y = `Proportion Correct`))+
  geom_jitter(alpha=0.2, width = 0.05, height = 0.05)+
  geom_smooth(method="loess", color = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    name = "",
    limits = c(8, 20), 
    breaks = seq(8, 20, by = 2)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1), 
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.25),
    labels = as.character
  ) +
  labs(title = "Auditory Discrimination")

print(auditory_plot)
```

#### Reproduce per-task models

##### Longitudinal only

```{r models_long}
task_models <- function(df) {
  
m_age <- glmer(cbind(`Trials Correct`, `Total Trials` - `Trials Correct`) ~ `Age (wks)` + (1 | `Dog ID`),
                 family = binomial, data = df)
m_exp <- glmer(cbind(`Trials Correct`, `Total Trials` - `Trials Correct`) ~ `Age (wks)` + experience + (1 | `Dog ID`),
                 family = binomial, data = df) 

tibble(AIC_age = AIC(m_age), AIC_age_exp = AIC(m_exp))
  }

aic_tibble <- bind_rows(
  "Marker gesture"               = task_models(marker_long),
  "Working memory (Delay)"       = task_models(workingmem_long),
  "Working memory (Distraction)" = task_models(distraction_long),
  "Auditory discrimination"      = task_models(auditory_long),
  "Odor discrimination"         = task_models(odor_long),
  "Cylinder: inhibitory control" = task_models(detour_long),
  "Cylinder: reversal learning"  = task_models(reversal_long),
  "Causal reasoning"             = task_models(causal_long),
  "Momentary pointing"           = task_models(momentary_long),
  .id="Task") |> 
  mutate(Best = if_else(AIC_age_exp < AIC_age, "age + experience", "age"))

aic_tibble

```

```{r proplook_models_long}

m_age <- glmer(cbind(`# Trials Looked`, `Total Trials` - `# Trials Looked`) ~ `Age (wks)` + (1 | `Dog ID`),
               family = binomial, data = unsolvable_long)
m_exp <- glmer(cbind(`# Trials Looked`, `Total Trials` - `# Trials Looked`) ~ `Age (wks)` + experience + (1 | `Dog ID`),
               family = binomial, data = unsolvable_long)

aic_tibble2 <- tibble(AIC_age = AIC(m_age), AIC_age_exp = AIC(m_exp))|>
  mutate(Best = if_else(AIC_age_exp < AIC_age, "age + experience", "age"))

aic_tibble2
```

```{r looktime_models_long}

m_age <- lmer(`Mean Look Time` ~ `Age (wks)` + (1 | `Dog ID`),
              data = unsolvable_long, REML = FALSE)
m_exp <- lmer(`Mean Look Time` ~ `Age (wks)` + experience + (1 | `Dog ID`),
              data = unsolvable_long, REML = FALSE)


aic_tibble3 <- tibble(AIC_age = AIC(m_age), AIC_age_exp = AIC(m_exp))|>
  mutate(Best = if_else(AIC_age_exp < AIC_age, "age + experience", "age"))

aic_tibble3
```

`correct ~ age + (1 | puppy_ID)` is better for:

- Marker Gesture (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble$AIC_age[aic_tibble$Task == "Marker gesture"], 1)`)

- Working Memory with Distraction (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble$AIC_age[aic_tibble$Task == "Working memory (Distraction)"], 1)`)

- Odor Discrimination (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble$AIC_age[aic_tibble$Task == "Odor discrimination"], 1)`)

- Unsolvable Proportion Looked (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble2$AIC_age, 1)`)

- Unsolvable Average Looking Time (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble3$AIC_age, 1)`).

`correct ~ age + experience + (1 | puppy_ID)` is better for:

- Working Memory with Delay (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble$Task == "Working memory (Delay)"], 1)`)

- Auditory Discrimination (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble$Task == "Auditory discrimination"], 1)`)

- Cylinder Inhibitory Control (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble$Task == "Cylinder: inhibitory control"], 1)`)

- Cylinder Reversal Learning (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble$Task == "Cylinder: reversal learning"], 1)`)

- Causal Reasoning (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble$Task == "Causal reasoning"], 1)`).

- Momentary Pointing (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble$Task == "Momentary pointing"], 1)`).

##### Longitudinal + Control, like paper

```{r models_all}
task_models2 <- function(df2) {
  
m_age <- glmer(cbind(`Trials Correct`, `Total Trials` - `Trials Correct`) ~ `Age (wks)` + (1 | `Dog ID`),
                 family = binomial, data = df2)
m_exp <- glmer(cbind(`Trials Correct`, `Total Trials` - `Trials Correct`) ~ `Age (wks)` + `# Prior Test Sessions` + (1 | `Dog ID`),
                 family = binomial, data = df2) 

tibble(AIC_age = AIC(m_age), AIC_age_exp = AIC(m_exp))
  }

aic_tibble4 <- bind_rows(
  "Marker gesture"               = task_models2(marker),
  "Working memory (Delay)"       = task_models2(workingmem),
  "Working memory (Distraction)" = task_models2(distraction),
  "Auditory discrimination"      = task_models2(auditory),
  "Odor discrimination"         = task_models2(odor),
  "Cylinder: inhibitory control" = task_models2(detour),
  "Cylinder: reversal learning"  = task_models2(reversal),
  "Causal reasoning"             = task_models2(causal),
  "Momentary pointing"           = task_models2(momentary),
  .id="Task") |> 
  mutate(Best = if_else(AIC_age_exp < AIC_age, "age + experience", "age"))

m_age <- glmer(cbind(`# Trials Looked`, `Total Trials` - `# Trials Looked`) ~ `Age (wks)` + (1 | `Dog ID`),
               family = binomial, data = unsolvable)
m_exp <- glmer(cbind(`# Trials Looked`, `Total Trials` - `# Trials Looked`) ~ `Age (wks)` + `# Prior Test Sessions` + (1 | `Dog ID`),
               family = binomial, data = unsolvable)

aic_tibble5 <- tibble(AIC_age = AIC(m_age), AIC_age_exp = AIC(m_exp))|>
  mutate(Best = if_else(AIC_age_exp < AIC_age, "age + experience", "age"))

aic_tibble5
```

```{r looktime_models_all}

m_age <- lmer(`Mean Look Time` ~ `Age (wks)` + (1 | `Dog ID`),
              data = unsolvable, REML = FALSE)
m_exp <- lmer(`Mean Look Time` ~ `Age (wks)` + `# Prior Test Sessions` + (1 | `Dog ID`),
              data = unsolvable, REML = FALSE)


aic_tibble6 <- tibble(AIC_age = AIC(m_age), AIC_age_exp = AIC(m_exp))|>
  mutate(Best = if_else(AIC_age_exp < AIC_age, "age + experience", "age"))

aic_tibble6
```

`correct ~ age + (1 | puppy_ID)` is better for:

- Marker Gesture (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble4$AIC_age[aic_tibble4$Task == "Marker gesture"], 1)`)

- Working Memory with Distraction (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble4$AIC_age[aic_tibble4$Task == "Working memory (Distraction)"], 1)`)

- Odor Discrimination (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble4$AIC_age[aic_tibble4$Task == "Odor discrimination"], 1)`)

- Momentary Pointing (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble4$AIC_age[aic_tibble4$Task == "Momentary Pointing"], 1)`)

`correct ~ age + experience + (1 | puppy_ID)` is better for:

- Working Memory with Delay (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble4$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble4$Task == "Working memory (Delay)"], 1)`)

- Auditory Discrimination (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble4$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble4$Task == "Auditory discrimination"], 1)`)

- Cylinder Inhibitory Control (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble4$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble4$Task == "Cylinder: inhibitory control"], 1)`)

- Cylinder Reversal Learning (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble4$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble4$Task == "Cylinder: reversal learning"], 1)`)

- Causal Reasoning (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble4$AIC_age_exp[aic_tibble4$Task == "Causal reasoning"], 1)`).

- Unsolvable Proportion Looked (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble5$AIC_age_exp, 1)`)

- Unsolvable Average Looking Time (AIC = `r round(aic_tibble6$AIC_age_exp, 1)`).

#### Confirmatory mixed-effects logistic model

```{r confirmatory_data}

all_tasks <- bind_rows(
  "Marker gesture"               = marker_long,
  "Working memory (Delay)"       = workingmem_long,
  "Working memory (Distraction)" = distraction_long,
  "Auditory discrimination"      = auditory_long,
  "Odor discrimination"          = odor_long,
  "Cylinder: inhibitory control" = detour_long,
  "Cylinder: reversal learning"  = reversal_long,
  "Causal reasoning"             = causal_long,
  "Momentary pointing"           = momentary_long,
  .id = "task") |>
  transmute(task,
            id      = factor(`Dog ID`),
            age     = `Age (wks)` - 8,
            correct = `Trials Correct`,
            total   = `Total Trials`)

ctrl <- glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))

r_age_exp <- bind_rows(marker_long, workingmem_long, distraction_long, auditory_long,
                       odor_long, detour_long, reversal_long, causal_long,
                       momentary_long, unsolvable_long) |>
  summarise(r = cor(`Age (wks)`, `# Prior Test Sessions`)) |>
  pull(r)

```

```{r model_buildup}
# random intercepts only
m1 <- glmer(cbind(correct, total - correct) ~ age * task + (1 | id) + (1 | id:task),
            family = binomial, data = all_tasks, control = ctrl)

# by-puppy random slope for age
m2 <- glmer(cbind(correct, total - correct) ~ age * task + (1 + age | id) + (1 | id:task),
            family = binomial, data = all_tasks, control = ctrl)

isSingular(m2)   # TRUE = random effects too complex for the data
anova(m1, m2)    # does the random slope improve fit?

# same slope as m2, no intercept-slope correlation
m3 <- glmer(cbind(correct, total - correct) ~ age * task + (1 + age || id) + (1 | id:task),
            family = binomial, data = all_tasks, control = ctrl)

isSingular(m3)    # FALSE = fitted cleanly
anova(m1, m3)     # no sig improvement, m1 has slightly better AIC

```

```{r interaction_test}
# m3 most complex model that converged without warnings
m_final <- m3

# KEY RESULT: age x task interaction
m_final_noint <- update(m_final, . ~ . - age:task)
lrt_m3 <-anova(m_final_noint, m_final)

# m1 has marginally lower AIC so using as robustness check
m_final2 <- m1

# age x task interaction
m_final2_noint <- update(m_final2, . ~ . - age:task)
lrt_m1 <- anova(m_final2_noint, m_final2)

```

```{r 113pups_exp}

all_tasks_all <- bind_rows(
  "Marker gesture"               = marker,
  "Working memory (Delay)"       = workingmem,
  "Working memory (Distraction)" = distraction,
  "Auditory discrimination"      = auditory,
  "Odor discrimination"          = odor,
  "Cylinder: inhibitory control" = detour,
  "Cylinder: reversal learning"  = reversal,
  "Causal reasoning"             = causal,
  "Momentary pointing"           = momentary,
  .id = "task") |>
  transmute(task,
            id         = factor(`Dog ID`),
            age        = `Age (wks)` - 8,
            experience = `# Prior Test Sessions`,
            correct    = `Trials Correct`,
            total      = `Total Trials`)

cor(all_tasks_all$age, all_tasks_all$experience)   #0.76

# Each task gets its own age slope AND its own experience slope
m_ae <- glmer(cbind(correct, total - correct) ~ age * task + experience * task +
                (1 | id) + (1 | id:task),
              family = binomial, data = all_tasks_all, control = ctrl)

# Does age x task matter AFTER accounting for task-specific experience effects?
m_ae_noint <- update(m_ae, . ~ . - age:task)
lrt_ae <- anova(m_ae_noint, m_ae)
lrt_ae
```

The age × task interaction was significant in the random-slope model (m3), \$\\chi\^2\$(`r lrt_m3$Df[2]`) = `r round(lrt_m3$Chisq[2], 2)`, p `r format.pval(lrt_m3$"Pr(>Chisq)"[2], digits = 2, eps = .001)`, and in the random-intercepts model (m1), \$\\chi\^2\$ (`r lrt_m1$Df[2]`) = `r round(lrt_m1$Chisq[2], 2)`, p `r format.pval(lrt_m1$"Pr(>Chisq)"[2], digits = 2, eps = .001)`. This indicates that the 9 tasks do not share one developmental rate, consistent with the multiple intelligences hypothesis. Because age and experience are highly correlated in the longitudinal puppies (r = `r round(r_age_exp, 2)`), this model cannot disentangle the model whether these task differences reflect maturation, accumulated testing experience, or both.

After adding the 22 control puppies and task-specific experience effects, the age × task interaction was still significant, \$\\chi\^2\$ (`r lrt_ae$Df[2]`) = `r round(lrt_ae$Chisq[2], 2)`, p `r format.pval(lrt_ae$"Pr(>Chisq)"[2], digits = 2, eps = .001)`. While part of the longitudinal age × task interaction effect may be shared with experience , the results from the 113-subject sample further support the multiple intelligences hypothesis, although age and experience remain partly correlated (r = `r round(cor(all_tasks_all$age, all_tasks_all$experience), 2)`).

#### Effect Sizes (Longitudinal)

```{r}
library(emmeans)

# slopes on the probability scale
slopes <- emtrends(m_final, ~ task, var = "age")
slopes_table <- as_tibble(slopes) |>
  mutate(OR_per_week = exp(age.trend))
slopes_table

# age slope per task on the log-odds scale
slopes_prob <- emtrends(m_final, ~ task, var = "age", regrid = "response")
slopes_prob

prob_table <- as_tibble(slopes_prob) |>
  select(task, prob_per_week = age.trend)

effect_table <- as_tibble(slopes) |>
  transmute(task,
            OR      = exp(age.trend),
            OR_low  = exp(asymp.LCL),
            OR_high = exp(asymp.UCL)) |>
  left_join(prob_table, by = "task") |>
  arrange(desc(OR)) |>
  transmute(Task = task,
            `OR per week [95% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", OR, OR_low, OR_high),
            `Change in proportion correct per week` = sprintf("%+.3f", prob_per_week))
effect_table
```

```{r pairwise}
# pairwise comparisons between tasks (Tukey-adjusted)
between_tasks <- as_tibble(pairs(slopes)) |>
  mutate(ratio_of_ORs = exp(estimate))
between_tasks

between_tasks_sig <- between_tasks |>
  mutate(sig = p.value<0.05) |>
  count(sig == "TRUE")
between_tasks_sig
```

Each task's age slope is reported as an odds ratio (OR) per week. Effects were largest for cylinder inhibitory control (OR \[95% CI\] = `r effect_table$"OR per week [95% CI]"[effect_table$Task == "Cylinder: inhibitory control"]`), cylinder reversal learning (OR = `r effect_table$"OR per week [95% CI]"[effect_table$Task == "Cylinder: reversal learning"]`), and causal reasoning (OR = `r effect_table$"OR per week [95% CI]"[effect_table$Task == "Causal reasoning"]`); smaller for marker gesture (OR = `r effect_table$"OR per week [95% CI]"[effect_table$Task == "Marker gesture"]`), working memory with distraction (OR = `r effect_table$"OR per week [95% CI]"[effect_table$Task == "Working memory (Distraction)"]`), and working memory with delay (OR = `r effect_table$"OR per week [95% CI]"[effect_table$Task == "Working memory (Delay)"]`); absent for momentary pointing (OR = `r effect_table$"OR per week [95% CI]"[effect_table$Task == "Momentary pointing"]`); and slightly negative for auditory discrimination (OR = `r effect_table$"OR per week [95% CI]"[effect_table$Task == "Auditory discrimination"]`) and odor discrimination (OR = `r effect_table$"OR per week [95% CI]"[effect_table$Task == "Odor discrimination"]`).

When using a probability scale to look at proportion correct by age, cylinder inhibitory control increased by about 4 percentage points per week, less than cylinder reversal learning (about 6 points per week), likely because scores already neared ceiling by mid-testing. Comparing tasks directly showed that most developed at significantly different rates (significant for 28 of 36 comparisons), again reflecting the multiple intelligences hypothesis. For example, cylinder inhibitory control improved `r round(between_tasks$ratio_of_ORs[between_tasks$contrast == "Cylinder: inhibitory control - Odor discrimination"], 2)` times faster per week than odor discrimination (p \< .001), whereas causal reasoning and reversal learning developed at similar rates (ratio = `r round(between_tasks$ratio_of_ORs[between_tasks$contrast == "Causal reasoning - Cylinder: reversal learning"], 2)`, p = `r round(between_tasks$p.value[between_tasks$contrast == "Causal reasoning - Cylinder: reversal learning"], 2)`).
